title: Occasion and date
short: Written near Milton's birthday (9 December), probably in 1632, and drafted in a letter to a friend who had chided him for delay.
body: The sonnet survives in the Trinity College (Cambridge) manuscript, copied into the draft of a letter to an unnamed friend who seems to have reproached Milton for idling in study instead of entering the ministry. Milton sends the sonnet as proof of his self-examination. It was printed in Poems (1645) and numbered VII in the 1673 edition. The date depends on how one reads 'three-and-twentieth year' (l. 2): the traditional dating is 9 December 1631, Milton's twenty-third birthday, but some editors prefer December 1632. Milton was then living at home after Cambridge, preparing through private study for a vocation as a poet.

title: the subtle thief of youth
short: Time personified as a sly thief that steals youth unnoticed.
body: 'Subtle' means crafty, stealthy. Time's theft of youth is a commonplace of Renaissance poetry, descending from Ovid's 'tempus edax rerum', time the devourer of things (Metamorphoses 15.234). Shakespeare's Sonnet 77 speaks of 'Time's thievish progress to eternity'. The pun in 'Stol'n' (l. 2) works both ways: time has stolen the year, and has stolen past him, quietly. The octave thus opens with Time as an enemy, a figure the sestet will reverse when Time 'leads' him (l. 12).

title: on his wing
short: Time is winged, the emblem of its swift flight.
body: Winged Time (often with scythe and hourglass) was a standard figure in Renaissance emblem books, and the proverb 'time flies' goes back to Virgil, 'fugit inreparabile tempus' (Georgics 3.284). Time carries off the year on its wing as a bird of prey carries its catch. Compare Job 9:25-26, where the speaker's days 'flee away' 'as the eagle that hasteth to the prey', which also anticipates 'hasting days' in l. 3.

title: my three-and-twentieth year
short: Either the year in which he turned twenty-three, or the year that ended on his twenty-third birthday; hence the dating dispute.
body: If the 'three-and-twentieth year' is the year that has just been stolen, Milton has completed it and is now twenty-three, which gives 9 December 1631, the traditional date (Luminarium and many chronologies). But the phrase can also be counted as the year he is living in, a twenty-third year that closes only on his twenty-fourth birthday, in December 1632, and some editors prefer that date. The evidence of the sonnet alone does not settle it. Either way it was written while Milton was living at home after Cambridge, and it goes with the letter to a friend preserved in the Trinity manuscript.

title: full career
short: At full gallop: a 'career' was a horse's charge at top speed, as in jousting.
body: The noun 'career' first meant a racecourse or the short gallop at full speed made in a tournament or the manege, hence 'in full career', headlong. The modern sense of a course of professional life had not yet developed, though for modern readers the word nicely anticipates the poem's concern with vocation. The days are 'hasting', hurrying, like the eagle in Job 9:26.

title: my late spring no bud or blossom
short: His youth is a late spring that has produced no flowers, i.e. no poetry worthy of him yet.
body: 'Late' means both recent (his spring has just passed) and belated (a slow spring). The plant image of bud and blossom, continued in 'ripeness' (l. 7), measures Milton's development as a poet in natural terms. He had already written the Nativity Ode, 'L'Allegro' and 'Il Penseroso', but by his own high standard none of this counted as the great work he intended. 'Shew'th' (shows) is contracted to one syllable so as to rhyme with 'youth' (l. 1), as 'endu'th' (l. 8) rhymes with 'truth' (l. 5).

title: semblance
short: His youthful outward appearance, which might hide how near to manhood he really is.
body: 'Semblance' is outward appearance. Milton looked young for his age: at Cambridge he was nicknamed 'the Lady of Christ's', partly for his delicate looks, and he alludes to the nickname in his sixth Prolusion. Lines 5-8 are hard to parse: perhaps my looks belie the fact that I am so near manhood, and inner maturity shows itself even less in me than it does in some more fortunate spirits who mature on time.

title: inward ripeness
short: Spiritual and intellectual maturity, as distinct from outward age; the image of ripening fruit.
body: Ripeness carries on the vegetable image of l. 4: the bud and blossom should lead to ripe fruit. The concept is central in Milton's thinking about readiness for vocation: in the letter that contains the sonnet he defends his delay as a deliberate preparation, not idleness. Compare Edgar's 'Ripeness is all' in King Lear 5.2, where ripeness also means a readiness that cannot be hurried and is in the hands of providence.

title: some more timely-happy spirits
short: People fortunate enough to mature early; whom Milton has in mind is unstated.
body: 'Timely-happy' means fortunate in timeliness, blessed with an early ripening. The phrase need not refer to anyone in particular, but it implies comparison with precocious contemporaries who had already made names for themselves. Editors have speculated about particular writers, but the poem gives no clue, and the general sense of envy and self-measurement is what matters. The hyphenated compound epithet is typical of Milton's early style.

title: endu'th
short: Endows, invests: inward ripeness is a gift bestowed on some spirits.
body: To 'endue' (or 'endow') is to furnish with a quality or gift; it overlaps with 'indue', to put on like a garment. The verb implies that ripeness is given, not earned, preparing for the sestet's appeal to 'grace' (l. 13). The rhyme with 'truth' (l. 5) completes the octave's two rhymes in the Italian manner (abba abba; 'shew'th' rhymes with 'youth'). The archaic -th ending, already old-fashioned by 1632, lends the line a grave, scriptural tone.

anchor: Yet be it less or more
title: The volta and Italian form
short: The turn: the sestet sets anxiety aside and trusts that his life is measured by Heaven.
body: The sonnet follows the Italian (Petrarchan) pattern Milton preferred: an octave abbaabba and a sestet cdedce, with no closing couplet. The volta at 'Yet' is clean: the octave laments outward and inner slowness, the sestet resolves it by submitting the question to Providence. The balanced pairs 'less or more, or soon or slow' and 'mean or high' sweep away the anxious comparisons of the octave. Milton had studied Italian sonneteers (Petrarch, Della Casa, Tasso) and had written Italian sonnets himself.

title: in strictest measure even
short: Exactly equal, matched precisely to the destiny God has in store.
body: 'Still' means always; 'ev'n' (one syllable) means level, exactly corresponding. Whatever his gifts ('it', the inward ripeness), they will always be exactly proportioned to the lot to which Time and God are leading him. 'Measure' may also suggest the measure of verse, a fitting pun for a poet, and the biblical idea that God measures each person's portion (compare 'with what measure ye mete', Matthew 7:2).

title: that same lot, however mean or high
short: The portion of life assigned by God, humble or exalted; 'lot' recalls the casting of lots and biblical inheritance.
body: A 'lot' is the share allotted, originally by the casting of lots, and in the Bible the inheritance God assigns (Psalm 16:5-6, 'thou maintainest my lot. The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places'). 'However mean or high' accepts in advance either a humble or a glorious calling. The modern reader knows that it would be high, but in 1632 Milton could not, and the poem's force lies in that uncertainty.

title: Time ... and the will of Heaven
short: Time is no longer a thief but a guide, leading him under Providence.
body: The sestet transforms the figure of Time from l. 1. There it was a thief; here it 'leads', in partnership with 'the will of Heav'n'. Time becomes an instrument of Providence rather than its enemy. The idea that each event comes at its due season echoes Ecclesiastes 3:1, 'To every thing there is a season'. The submission anticipates the patient waiting of Sonnet 19's last line.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Ecclesiastes 3:1

anchor: All is, if I have grace
title: All is, if I have grace to use it so
short: The famous compressed ending, read in several ways; all turn on using one's gift as if always in God's sight.
body: The syntax is elliptical and has been much debated. One reading: 'All that matters is whether I have grace to use my lot as one ever in God's sight'. Another: 'All is (as it has always been) in God's eye, provided I have grace to use it'. A third takes 'All is ... as ever' to mean that everything, including his slow growth, is eternally seen and ordered by God. On every reading, success depends on grace, God's unmerited gift, rather than on Milton's own effort or timing; the poem's anxiety about achievement is answered by the theology of grace.

title: my great Task-Master's eye
short: God as the master who assigns work and will call his servants to account, as in the parable of the talents.
body: The image recalls the Gospel parables of service: the master who gives talents to his servants and on return demands an account (Matthew 25:14-30), and the householder who hires labourers at different hours yet pays them alike (Matthew 20:1-16), which suits a man worried about being late. In Exodus 'taskmasters' are the Egyptian overseers (Exodus 1:11), but Milton's 'great' Task-Master is just and watchful, not cruel. The thought returns, darker, in Sonnet 19 ('When I consider how my light is spent'), with its 'one talent which is death to hide' and its question whether God exacts 'day-labour, light denied'.
